items.title: A guitar string vibrates at all its harmonics at once
items.claim: Pluck a guitar string. The note you hear has a fundamental frequency (say 110 Hz for an A2). But the string actually vibrates simultaneously in all the modes allowed by its end constraints: the fundamental, twice it (220 Hz), three times (330 Hz), and so on. The relative strengths of these harmonics give the guitar its sound.
items.prompt: Why these specific frequencies and no others?

options.text: The string is fixed at both ends; allowed standing waves must have nodes at the endpoints, which restricts wavelengths to 2L/n where L is string length and n is an integer. Each n gives a different harmonic frequency
The string can only oscillate as a whole
The amplifier adds the harmonics electronically

items.reveal:
A string of length L fixed at both ends supports standing waves only if a whole number of half-wavelengths fits in the length: λ_n = 2L/n. The corresponding frequencies are f_n = n × v / (2L), where v is the wave speed along the string. The lowest mode (n=1) is the fundamental; n=2 is the first overtone (twice the fundamental); and so on.

The shape of a plucked string is the superposition of these allowed modes. The way you pluck (where and how) determines which modes get excited and with what amplitudes.

This is the simplest example of how boundary conditions select discrete energy levels in quantum mechanics. A particle confined to a box has discrete energies because its wavefunction must satisfy similar conditions at the box walls. Music and quantum mechanics are mathematically twins.
items.why: Strings are taught as 'they vibrate'. They vibrate in a specific spectrum dictated by their length and tension — and that spectrum is foundational to everything from music to spectroscopy.

items.title: A bridge tore itself apart from a steady wind
items.claim: On 7 November 1940 the Tacoma Narrows Bridge in Washington State collapsed after four months in service. A wind of about 19 m/s set the deck twisting at its torsional natural frequency. Within hours, the oscillation built up to several metres of amplitude and the structure failed.
items.prompt: How can a steady wind cause unbounded oscillation?

options.text: The wind happened to gust at exactly the right frequency
Aeroelastic flutter — the bridge's torsional motion changed the air flow in a way that fed energy back into the same motion at the same frequency, amplifying every cycle
The wind was much stronger than reported

items.reveal:
Driven resonance: a periodic external force at the natural frequency drives the oscillation higher each cycle. The amplitude grows linearly with time (limited by damping).

Aeroelastic flutter is different and more dangerous: the structure's own motion alters the airflow, which then drives the motion at the same frequency. It's a feedback loop where the driving frequency automatically locks to the response frequency. A steady wind suffices.

The Tacoma Narrows deck was an aerodynamically simple H-shape with a high aspect ratio. It was particularly vulnerable to torsional flutter at moderate wind speeds.

London's Millennium Bridge in 2000 had a similar story but with pedestrians instead of wind. Walkers' lateral footfalls synchronised with the bridge's natural side-to-side mode; the crowd unconsciously walked in step and amplified the swaying. The bridge was closed and dampers fitted.
items.why: Resonance is taught as benign (musical instruments). Aeroelastic flutter is its destructive cousin — and engineers must design against it explicitly.

items.title: Transformers can be over 99 percent efficient — better than almost any machine
items.claim: A large power-station step-up transformer is around 99.5 percent efficient. A typical car engine is about 25 percent. Most domestic appliances are 30-80 percent. Transformers convert AC voltage with almost no loss.
items.prompt: How is a passive iron-and-copper device so efficient?

options.text: It contains no moving parts to wear out

Transformers have no thermodynamic Carnot limit because they don't go via heat — they exchange energy magnetically by mutual induction; losses are limited to ohmic heating in windings, eddy currents and core hysteresis
They store energy and return it later

items.reveal:
A transformer has two coils wound around a shared iron core. AC in the primary creates an oscillating magnetic flux through the core; the flux induces an EMF in the secondary equal to V_secondary = (N_secondary / N_primary) × V_primary.

Losses come from: (1) ohmic heating in the windings (I squared R), (2) eddy currents induced in the iron core (suppressed by laminating the core into thin insulated sheets), (3) hysteresis losses as the iron magnetises and demagnetises 100 times per second (50 Hz, both polarities).

A well-designed transformer at full load loses about 0.5 percent. Empty (no load on secondary), losses fall to a fraction of a percent. The same physics underlies wireless phone chargers — inductive coupling at higher frequencies.
items.why: Transformers look passive and boring. They are among the most efficient energy-conversion devices humans have ever built.
